Let’s talk about something that often sneaks up on people, sometimes so quietly that you only see it looking back. Chapter 5: Early Warning Signs—How Control and Devaluation Begin.
Think about those moments when things just felt a little off. Maybe it was a sarcastic comment that hit harder than you expected, or suddenly having to explain where you were every minute you were apart. At first, these things might seem minor—easy to ignore, or even justify. But looking back, they’re often the very first cracks in the foundation.
One story stands out. Picture this: someone’s partner makes jokes about her appearance or her intelligence in front of friends. At first, she laughs along, not wanting to be the one who “can’t take a joke.” But soon, the jokes get sharper. The laughter? It starts to feel forced. And when she tries to say something, he turns it around—says she’s just being too sensitive.
Or maybe you’ve heard about the partner who always needs to know where someone is. The calls and texts keep coming, all under the guise of “just making sure you’re safe.” If she pushes back, suddenly he’s upset, or accuses her of not caring enough. Slowly, without even realizing, she starts canceling plans or avoiding friends—just to avoid another argument.
What’s tricky is, these early warning signs are often wrapped up in words that sound like love or concern. “I just care about you so much,” or, “I can’t help it if I get jealous.” The control is hidden, dressed up as devotion, and that makes it tough to spot for what it really is.
There’s something else that happens, too: devaluation. Over time, a controlling partner might start chipping away at your confidence. Maybe it’s criticizing your choices, dismissing your opinions, or making you feel silly for sharing your needs. Sometimes it’s subtle—a rolled eye during a conversation. Other times, it’s more direct—name-calling, or even questioning your sanity.
Here’s something to pay attention to: these behaviors don’t usually happen all at once. They build up, little by little, making it easy to brush off or downplay each new thing. And by the time you notice the pattern, you might already feel stuck or unsure about what to do next.
Spotting these signs early is so important. It gives you a chance to set boundaries, reach out for support, and make decisions before things get even harder. And maybe most importantly, it helps break that sense of isolation so many people feel. When you realize you’re not alone, when you see that others have gone through the same thing, it suddenly feels easier to ask for help.
Healing starts with awareness. When you can name what’s happening and really see the mindset behind it, you begin to reclaim your sense of self. And remember—missing those early signs doesn’t mean it’s your fault. It’s about learning to trust your instincts again, and knowing, deep down, that everyone deserves respect and kindness.
